desc:
An undirected graph has vertices 0..n-1 and the edge list edges, where every [u, v] joins two different vertices. Give each vertex a color so that the two ends of every edge have different colors.

Return the smallest number of colors that makes this possible (the chromatic number of the graph).

n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]]            →  3   (a triangle)
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,0]]      →  2   (a 4-cycle)
n = 5, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[4,0]] →  3   (an odd cycle)
constraints: No self-loops and no repeated edges; the graph may be disconnected
hints: Turn the question into a yes/no one: can the graph be colored with k colors? Ask it for k = 1, 2, 3, ... The first k that works is the answer, and k = n always works.

To test a fixed k, color vertices one by one with backtracking: a vertex may take any color not used by an already colored neighbour. Avoid repeating mirror-image work: a vertex may open a new color only if it is the next unused one (colors are interchangeable).

The order of the vertices decides the speed. Always continue with the uncolored vertex that currently sees the most different colors among its neighbours (ties: the larger degree). Such vertices fail early, which prunes the tree a lot (this is the DSATUR heuristic).
editorial: The chromatic number is found by testing k = 1, 2, 3, ... until a proper coloring with k colors exists. With no edges the answer is 1, otherwise at least 2. The test for a fixed k is a backtracking search: choose a vertex, try every allowed color, recurse, undo.

Two ideas make it fast enough for n ≤ 15. First, symmetry: colors are interchangeable, so a vertex may use an already used color or exactly one new color (the smallest unused one); this removes a factor of up to k! from the search. Second, dynamic vertex ordering: choose the uncolored vertex whose neighbours already use the most distinct colors (its saturation), breaking ties by degree. Such vertices have few options, so contradictions appear after a few levels. The worst case is still exponential, as the problem is NP-hard.
time: O(n * k^n) worst case, far less with pruning
